text.head: A DESCRIPTIVE POEM ADDRESSED TO TWO LADIES At their Return from Viewing The Mines near Whitehaven, to which are added SOME THOUGHTS ON BUILDING AND PLANTING TO Sir James Lowther of Lowther-Hall, Bart. By JOHN DALTON, D.D.
text.p: LONDON: Printed for J. And J. RIVINGTON in St. Paul’s Church-yard, and R. And J. DODSLEY in Pall-Mall. MDCCLV.

chap.title: PREFACE
chap.head: PREFACE

p.i:
The following Poem was written almo∫t two years ago, and was not intended for the pre∫s: but the approbation, with which ∫everal friends of the author have peru∫ed it, now encourages him to offer it to the public. It was owing to the ∫trong inclination, by which he was prompted to expre∫s the plea∫ure he had received, in a vi∫it paid to his native country after a long ab∫ence, from the view of ∫everal uncommon, grand, or beautiful ∫cenes of nature and of art, which he here attempts to de∫cribe. This plea∫ure was undoubtedly much benighted by an advantagious compari∫on of its pre∫ent ∫tate with That, in which he had left it. When we behold rich improvements of a wild and uncultivated ∫oil, in their ∫tate of maturity, without having ob∫erved their ri∫e and progre∫s, we are ∫truck with wonder and a∫toni∫hment, to ∫ee the face of Nature totally changed. It carries an air of enchantment and romance: and the fabulous and luxuriant de∫cription, given is by the Poet, of yellow harve∫ts ri∫ing up in∫tantaneou∫ly under the wheels of the chariot of Ceres,
as it pa∫∫ed over the barren de∫erts, hardly ∫eems, in the mid∫t of our ∫urpri∫e, too extravagant an image to repre∫ent the greatne∫s and ∫eeming ∫uddenne∫s of ∫uch a change:

But how great and rational ∫oever the plea∫ure of ∫uch a ∫ight may be, it is ∫till ∫urpa∫∫ed by that ari∫ing from the extraordinary increa∫e of a trading Town, and the new plantations of Hou∫es and Men. Such was the ∫ati∫faction the author felt at the appearance of the town and harbour of Whitehaven, after an ab∫ence of ∫omewhat le∫s than thirty years. The Mines near that place are remarkable for ∫o many ∫ingular circum∫tances, that they are generally e∫teemed to be well worth the ob∫ervation of travellers. But the uncommonne∫s of the occa∫ion, on which this de∫cription was addre∫∫ed by two very amiable Per∫ons, afforded him the means of ∫till heightening the novelty of his ∫ubject, and of throwing it into a more agreeable and poetic light by an early introduction of cla∫∫ical allu∫ion and parody . It al∫o gave him (what he valued
mo∫t) a natural opportunity of expre∫∫ing his ju∫t e∫teem for a truly re∫pectable family, with who∫e merit he had long had the happine∫s of being well acquainted, who∫e Intere∫t appears to be in∫eparably connected with That of his native country, and to which It already owed the mo∫t con∫iderable advantages.

chap.note:
Allu∫ion and parody &c.] To ∫ave the reader the trouble of turning to books, ∫everal of the pa∫∫ages alluded to in the de∫cription of the mines are here in∫erted:
quae te fortuna fatigat, Ut tri∫tes ∫ine ∫ole domos, loca turbida, adires? Virg. Æn. VI At cantu commotae Erebi de fedibus imis Umbrae ibant tenues, ∫imulcraq; luce carentum Quin ip∫ae ∫tupere domus, atq; intima Lethi Tartara, coeruleo∫q; implexae crinibus angues Eumenides; tenuitq; inihans tria Cerebus ora; Atq; Ixionii cantu rota con∫titit orbis.Virg.Georg.Lib.IV. ulla ∫it immunis regio, nullamq; ∫ub urbis Pectus inacce∫∫um Veneri. Jam tri∫tis Eryannis Seniat ardores: Acheron, Diti∫q, ∫everi ferrea la∫civis molle∫cant corda ∫agittis.Claud.de Rap.prof.Lib.I. divino femita gre∫∫u Claruit. Hinc exaudiri gemitus, & ∫aeva ∫onare Verbera: tum ∫tridor ferri, tractaeq; catenae. Virg.Æn.Lib.VI Hine via Tartarii quae fert Acerontis ad undas Turbidus hine coeno ra∫taq; voragine gurges Æ∫tuat, atq; omnem Cocyto eructat arenam. Virg.Æn.Lib.VI

p.i:
The admirers of the exten∫ive knowledge, un∫potted honour, public ∫pirit, and firm adherence to the great and e∫∫ential intere∫ts of the Briti∫h con∫titution and Prote∫tant Succe∫∫ion, by which the late Lord Lon∫dale
was univer∫ally di∫tingui∫hed, may perhaps be offended at the author's confirming him∫elf, in what he here ∫ays of his Lord∫hip, to his provincial character; to his improvements in hu∫bandry, and his endeavours to introduce manufactures into his own country. His excu∫e mu∫t be, that this was the part of his Lord∫hip's Character which came mo∫t properly within the compa∫s of his ∫ubject. Be∫ides if the light in which he has endeavoured to place his Example in that particular, could, in any degree, contribute to engage the imitation of young per∫ons of the ∫ame rank and fortune in other places, he might then hope that the moral of his poem would appear to be not entirely provincial but national.

For, during the pre∫ent melancholy condition, even in an age eminent for charity, of the numerous unemployed Poor of this Kingdom, and the experienced and acknowledged inability of the pre∫ent laws to provide for their effectual employment at home, and to prevent their crowding into this their great ∫chool of idlene∫s and vice, the Metropolis, what can we hope for, to alleviate this mi∫ery, but that Noblemen and Gentlemen of con∫iderable e∫tates, daily growing more ∫en∫ible of the nece∫∫ity of ∫uch a conduct, will lend a like generous attention to eh ignorance and poverty of their re∫pective countrymen? This, as far as the author can pre∫ume to judge of ∫o difficult a matter, appears to be the be∫t that can be done, untill the Legi∫lature ∫hall be ∫o happy as to accompli∫h that great and by ∫ome ∫uch ∫imple yet comprehen∫ive plan, as was, in a late ∫e∫∫ion of parliament, recommend to their con∫ideration by a Noble Earl;
and which met with their mo∫t favourable reception at that time, though it has not yet received the ∫anction of a law.

This preface mu∫t not conclude without a precaution to the Raeder, which may po∫∫ibly prevent his meeting with an unplea∫ing di∫appointment. If , by the imperfect ∫ketch in the following Poem, or by what he may el∫ewhere hear of the vale of Ke∫wick and lake of Derwentwater, he ∫hould be induced to vi∫it the Original, he mu∫t not confidently expect to ∫ee it exactly in the ∫tate de∫cribed. For, if he goes thither with an imagination glowing warm with cla∫∫ical enthu∫ia∫m and expects to find the ∫ylvan ∫hrines of rural divinities wholly undi∫turbed and unprofaned, he will be much mi∫taken. In∫tead of that, he mu∫t prepare to be ∫hocked at ∫ome late violations if tho∫e ∫acred woods and groves, which had, for ages ∫haded the ∫ide of the ∫urrounding mountains, and (if pro∫e be allowed the expre∫∫ion) the ∫hores and promontories of that lovely lake. For

poem.line: Where the rude axe with heaved ∫troke
Was never heard the Nymphs to daunt
Or fright them from their hallow'd haunt,
A voice of weepng heard and loud lamet;
The Nymphs in twilight ∫hade of tangled thickets mourn.

p.i: However, for his con∫olation, he may ∫till, notwith∫tanding all tho∫e profanations, hope to find there an a∫∫emblage of ∫uch exqui∫ite though different beauties, as will well de∫erve to be admired by him; as well perhaps as any one part of the inanimate creation.

chap.title: TO TWO LADIES
chap.head: TO TWO LADIES At their Return from Viewing The Mines near Whitheaven.

poem.line: Thrice welcome to the balmy air
poem.note: From ∫ulphurous damps, &c.]The coals mines near Whitehaven are greatly infe∫ted with fulminating damps; large quantities of them being frequently collected in tho∫e de∫erted works, which are not ventilated with perpetual currents of fre∫h air: and, in ∫uch works, they often remain for a long time, without doing any mi∫chief. But when, by ∫ome accident, they are ∫et on fire, they then produce dreadful explo∫ions, very de∫tructive to the miners; and bur∫ting out of the pits with great impetuo∫ity, like the fiery eruptions from burning mountains, force along with them ponderous bodies to as great height in the air
poem.line: Till to the frighted realms of day
Thro' flaming mouths they force their way;
From the dark man∫ions of de∫pair
Welcome once more to light and air!
BUT why explore that world of night
Such grace and beauty why confine
One moment to a dreary mine?
WAS it becau∫e your curious eye
poem.note: From burning rocks &c.] The coal in the∫e mines hath, ∫everal times, been ∫et on fire by the fulminating damp, and hath continued burning for many months; until large ∫treams of water were conducted into the mines, and ∫uffered to fill tho∫e parts where the coal was on fire. By ∫uch fires, ∫everal collieries have been intirely de∫troyed; of which there are in∫tances near Newca∫tle, and in other parts of England, and in the ∫hore of Fife in Scotland; in ∫ome of which places, the fire has continued burning for ages. But more mines have been ruined by inundations.
poem.line: How bubbling fountains learn to flow?
OR rather that the ∫ons of day
And therefore, like young Ammon, you
While you the cavern'd hill de∫cend,
Tho', warn'd by him, with bended head
With cautious foot the rugged way,
Tho' he with hundred gates and chains
The Demons of the mine re∫trains,
poem.note: The demons of the mine re∫trains, &c.]In order to prevent, as much as po∫∫ible the collieries from being filled with tho∫e pernicious damps, if has been found nece∫∫ary carefully to ∫earch for tho∫e crevices in coal, from whence they i∫∫ue out; and at tho∫e places, to confine them within a narrow ∫pace; and from tho∫e narrow ∫paces in which they are confined, to conduct them through long pipes into the open air; where being ∫et on fire, they con∫ume in perpetual flames, as they continually ari∫e out of the earth.
poem.line: To whom their parent, jealous Earth,
To guard her hidden ∫tores gave birth,
With hideous joy pale Orcus rung;
Tho' boiling with vain rage they ∫it
Fix'd to the bottom of the pit,
While at his beck the ∫pi'rits of air
With breath of heaven their taints repair;
Thro' ways a∫∫ign'd by him they ri∫e
Troop after troop at day expire
poem.note: And ∫ummons &c.] Tho∫e who have the direction of the∫e deep and exten∫ive works are obliged to u∫e great care and art in keeping them continually ventilated with perpetual currents of fre∫h air; which afford the miners a con∫tant ∫upply of that vital fluid, and expel out of the mines damps and other noxious exhalations together with ∫uch other burnt and foul air; as is become poi∫onous and unfit for re∫piration.
poem.line: The public care and wonder go
Of all above and all below.
FOR at your preference toil is o'er,
The re∫tle∫s miner works no more.
Nor ∫trikes the flint, nor whirls the ∫teel
Which, form'd by Pro∫pero's magic care,
poem.note: Nor ∫trikes the flint &c.]It having been ob∫erved by Mr. Spedding, who ∫uperintends the∫e collieries, and to whom the author here give the name of Pro∫pero, that the fulminating damp could only be kindled by flame, and that it was not liable to be ∫et on fire but red-hot iron, not by the ∫park produced by the colli∫ion of flint and ∫teel, he invented a machine, in which a ∫teel wheel is turned round with a very rapid motion, and flint are applied thereto, great plenty of fiery ∫parks are emitted, that afford the miners ∫uch a light as enables them to carry on their work in clo∫e places, where are the flames of a candle, or lamp, would occa∫ion dreadful explo∫ions. Without ∫ome invention of this ∫ort, the working of the∫e mines, ∫o greatly annoyed with their inflameable damps, would long ago have been impracticable.
poem.line: And make the gri∫ly cavern bright.
But quits it now, and ha∫tes away
De∫cend to him from fields of air.
Of gloomy Dis, the infernal god,
With pity when th' Orphean lyre
BUT on you move thro' ways le∫s ∫teep
To loftier chambers of the deep,
Mines that o'er mines by flights a∫cend.
poem.note: But on you move, &c.] The reader may ∫uppo∫e that he hath entered the∫e mines by an opening in the bottom of a hill, and hath already pa∫∫ed through a long adit hewn in the rock, and arched over with rock which is the principal road into them for men, and for hor∫es; and which, by a deep de∫cent, leads down to the lowe∫t vein of coal. Being arrived at the coal he may ∫uppo∫e him∫elf ∫till to de∫cend, by ways le∫s ∫teep, till, after a journey of a mile and a half, he arrives at the profounde∫t parts of the mine. The greate∫t part of this de∫cent is through ∫pacious galleries, which continually inter∫ect other galleries; all the coal being cut away except large pillars, which in deep parts of the mine, are three yards high, and about twelve yards ∫quare at the ba∫e; ∫uch great ∫trength being there required to ∫upport the ponderous roof.

A triple ∫tory, &c.]There are here three ∫trata of coal, which lie at a con∫iderable di∫tance one above another. The mines wrought in the∫e parallel ∫trata have a communication by pits, and are compared by the author to the different ∫tories of a building.
poem.line: But who in order can relate
How in clo∫e center of the∫e mines,
Nor the wing'd Zephyrs e're re∫ort,
How, breathle∫s, with faint pace, and ∫low
Thro' her grim ∫ultry realm you go,
poem.note: Thick Acherontic rivers, &c.]The water that flows from the coal is collected into one ∫tream, which runs towards the fire-engines. The water is yellow and turbid, from a mixture of ocher, and ∫o very corro∫ive, that it quickly con∫umes iron.

How, breathle∫s, with faint pace, and ∫low, &c.] Tho∫e who de∫cend into the∫e mines, find them mo∫t clo∫e and ∫ultry in the middle parts, there are mo∫t remote from the pits and adits, and perceive them to grow cooler the nearer they approach to tho∫e pits which are ∫unk to the deepe∫t parts of the mines; down which pits, large ∫treams of fre∫h air are made to de∫cend, and up which, the water is drawn out, by means of fire engines.
poem.line: Your progre∫s next the wondering mu∫e
Where Earth, the miner's way to clo∫e,
Did once his ma∫∫y rock oppo∫e
In vain: his daring axe he heaves,
To'wards the black view a pa∫∫age cleaves:
Thus, urg'd by Hunger's clamorous call,
poem.note: Where Earth, &c.] The vein of coal is not always regularly continued in the ∫ame inclined plain, but , in∫tead, thereof, the miners frequently meet with hard rock which interrupts their further progre∫s. At ∫uch places there ∫eem to have been breaks in the earth, from the ∫urface downwards; one part of the earth ∫eeming to have ∫unk down, while the part adjoining has remained in its ancient ∫ituation. In ∫ome of the places , the earth may have ∫unk ten or twenty fathoms, or more; in other places le∫s than one fathom. The∫e breaks, the miners call Sykes; and when they come at one of them, their fir∫t care is to di∫cover whether the ∫trata in the part adjoining be higher or lower than in the part where they have been working; or (to u∫e their own terms) whether the coal be ca∫t down, or ca∫t up. If it be ca∫t down, they ∫ink a pit to it; but if it be ca∫t up to any con∫iderable height, they are oftentimes obliged, with great labour and expence, as at the place here de∫cribed, to carry forward a level of long gallery thro' the rock until they again arrive at the ∫tratum of coal.
poem.line: In ∫pacious rooms once more you tread,
Whole roofs with figures quaint o'er∫pread
Wild nature paints with various dyes,
Down to the cold and humid caves,
Where hi∫∫ing fall the turbid waves.
The clank of chains your ears invades.
Thro' pits profound from di∫tant day
Scarce travels down light's languid ray.
High on huge axis heav'd above,
poem.note: Whole roofs, &c.] The∫e colours, with which the free-∫tone roof of the mine is beautifully variegated in many places, and which have the appearance of clouds, ∫eem to proceed from exudations of ∫alts, ocher and other earthy ∫ub∫tances.
poem.line: While pent within the iron womb
Of boiling cauldrons pants for room
As cold re∫trains, or heat impells,
poem.note: While pent within the iron womb, &c.]The author hath here taken occa∫ion to celebrate the fire-engine, the invention of which does ∫uch honour to this nation. He has endeavoured to de∫cribe, in a poetic manner, the effects of the ela∫tic ∫team and the great power of the atmo∫phere; which by their alternate actions, give force and motion to the beam of this engine, and by it, to the pump rods, which elevate the water through tubes, and di∫charge it out the mine. It appears, from pretty exact calculations, that it would require about 550 men, or a power equal to that of 110 hor∫es, to work the pump of one of the large∫t fire-engines now in u∫e, (the diameter of who∫e cylinder is ∫eventy inches) and thrice that number of men to keep an engine of this ∫ize con∫tantly at work. And that as much water may be rai∫ed by an engine of this ∫ize kept con∫tantly at work, as can be drawn up by 2520 men with rollers and buckets, after the manner now daily practiced in many mines; or as much as can be borne upon the ∫houlders of twice that number of men; as is ∫aid to be done in ∫ome of the mines of Peru. So great is the power of the air in one of tho∫e engines. There are four fire-engines belonging to this colliery; which, when all at work, di∫charge from it about 1228 gallons every minute, at thirteen ∫trokes; 1,768,320 gallons every twenty-four hours. By the four here employed, nearly twice the above mentioned quantity of water might be di∫charged from mines that are not above ∫ixty or ∫eventy fathoms deep, which depth is rarely exceeded in the Newca∫tle collieries, or in any of the Engli∫h collieries, tho∫e of Whitehaven excepted. the reader may find an account of Savery's engines in Harris's Lexicon Technicum. Many great improvements have been made to it ∫ince, and are daily making; ∫everal of which are related in the Philo∫ophical Tran∫actions. The be∫t account of it, its various improvements and u∫es is, I think, in Dr. De∫agulier's cour∫e of experimental philo∫ophy. vol. II.
poem.line: Pumps moved by rods from ponderous beams
Fire, water, air, heat, cold unite,
Or deepe∫t mines from flood defend
Man's riche∫t gift thy work will ∫hine;
Rome's aqueducts were poor to thine!
AT la∫t the long de∫cent if o'er;
Above your heads the bellows roar;
High o'er your heads they roar in vain;
Not all the ∫urges of the main
The dark rece∫s can e're di∫clo∫e,
Rocks heap'd in rocks th' attempt oppo∫e:
Thrice Dover's cliff from you the tides
Invade no more the realms of night.
Once to have left their azure ∫kies.
poem.note: Above your heads, &c.] The mines are here ∫unk to a depth of one under and thirty fathoms and are extended under the ∫ea to places where there is above them ∫ufficient depth of water for ∫hips of large burden. The∫e are the deepe∫t coal mines that have hitherto been wrought; and perhaps the miners have not in any other part of the globe, penetrated to ∫o great a depth below the ∫urface of the ∫ea; the very deep mines in Hungary, Peru and el∫ewhere , being ∫ituated in mountainous countries, where the ∫urface of the earth is elevated to a great height above the level of the ocean.
poem.line: heroes them∫elves, in days of yore,
Bold as they were, achiev'd no more.
Without a dread de∫cent you may
As with an ea∫y eye look down
On that fair port and happy town.
And his poor bark un∫helter'd lay,
Now lofty piers their arms extend,
The fury of the roaring main.
The peopl'd vale fair dwellings fill,
Brings all her honey to the hive,
Example works th' effect of law,
THESE are the glories of the mine!
poem.note: The glories of the mine, &c.] The∫e mines were fi∫t wrought , for foreign con∫umption by Sir John Lowther, Bart. one of the Lords of the Admiralty in the reign of King William; a per∫on of great abilities and a generous benefactor to his native country; who, by the encouragements which he gave to trade∫men and artificers of all kinds to ∫ettle at Whitehaven, may be e∫teemed the founder of that how. His ∫on and ∫ucce∫∫or, Sir James Lowther, pur∫uing the ∫ame plan, has brought the∫e mines to their pre∫ent ∫tate of perfection. It has been computed , that the∫e two gentlemen, in the compa∫s of a century (which time they have enjoyed the∫e mines) have expended in one of them only upwards of half a million ∫terling. -- The money returned hither for coals exported hence, greatly contributes to enable this remote country to pay tho∫e large ∫ums, that are continually drained out of it in taxes and cu∫toms, in rents to ab∫entees, and for clothing and various other nece∫∫ary commodities, which tho∫e parts do not afford. -- By this trade, and its con∫equences, the town of Whitehaven has been rai∫ed, from very low beginnings to its pre∫ent ∫tate; the country round it improved; and great numbers of hardy ∫ailors, and other u∫eful artificers trained up to ∫erve their King and country in the navy, as well as in the home and foreign trades of the kingdom.
poem.line: Delight to every eye and heart,
Your native Stream his charms di∫play
To court you to his banks again;
Now wind in wanton waves his train,
Then hid by pendent rocks would ∫teal,
But tuneful Falls his cour∫e reveal,
As down the bending vale he roves
Thro Yanwath woods and Buckholme's groves;
Warbling he flows, while Zephyrs breathe.
Where bounds the buck, and ∫kips the fawn,
poem.note: your native ∫tream, &c.]The river Lowther.
Then bid by pendent rocks, &c.] See in Mr Dalton's drawings, a view of this river near the bridge and church of A∫kham.
As down the bending vale &c.] See his view (taken from Clifton) of the river winding between Yanwath and Buckholme woods round the Ely∫ian fields.
See his view, on a ∫mall ∫cale taken from A∫kham Fell, of the ∫ituation of Lowther-hall, park etc. terminated by a long range of very high mountains called Cro∫s-fell.
poem.line: or couch'd beneath the hawthorn trees,
In dappled groups enjoy the breeze.
An oak for many an age has ∫tood
While men and herds, with ∫wift decay,
Race after race, have pa∫s'd away.
Huge boughs, which round o'erhang the plain,
Where flocks and herds at ea∫e repo∫e!
THERE the brown fells a∫cend the ∫ky,
On azure roofs bright ∫un beams play,
And make the meane∫t dwelling gay.
Thus oft the wife all-ruling mind
Is to the lowly cottage kind,
Bids there Hi∫s beams of favour fall,
That This may hear his awful frown,
And grateful That his goodne∫s own.
To chance the ∫cene: To nature's pride,
Sweet Ke∫wick's vale, the u∫e will guide.
The mu∫e who trod th'inchanted ground,
With you will ha∫te once more to hail
poem.note: On azure roofs &c.]The hou∫es of this country are covered with a beautiful blue ∫late.
poem.line: Be thou the Mu∫e's favourite theme:
Their painted heads the lillies re∫t,
To where in deep capacious bed
Down the rough rocks of dread Lodore
And foaming rend the frighted deep,
poem.note: Of dread Lodore, &c.] A very high ca∫cade here fall ∫in to the lake of Derwentwater near where Borrodale-beck (or brook) enters into it as is de∫cribed above.
poem.line: Thro thine own native dale, where ri∫e
HORRORS like the∫e at fir∫t alarm,
And rai∫e to noble∫t though the mind:
Thus by thy fall, Lodore, reclin'd
Who∫e ∫hadows mix o'er half the flood,
Scarce lifted by the languid gale
O'er the cap'd hill, and darken'd vale;
The ravening kite, and bird of Jove,
Which round th' aerial ocean rove,
Their flutt'ring or their bleating prey
Rocks to the lake in thunder born
Or ∫uch as o'er our heads appear
Who rules fire, water, air and land,
I view with wonder and delight,
For, ∫ee with them, the verdant I∫les
More tempting twine their opening bowers,
More lively glow their purple flowers,
In fairer circle bends the bay,
poem.note: Channels by rocky torrents torn, &c.] For an account of an extraordinary ∫torm in a part of this country called St. John's Vale, but which numerous fragments of rocks were driven down from the mountains, along with cataracts of water, ∫ee a letter from Cockermouth, in∫erted in Gentleman's Magazine of October 1754.
poem.line: And la∫t, to fix our wand'ring eyes,
Thy roofs, O Ke∫wick, brighter ri∫e
The lake and lofty hills between,
To whom all Britain ∫inks a vale!
And thence -- My Mu∫e, the∫e flights forbear,
Nor with wild raptures tire the fair.
Hills, rocks and dale have been too long
poem.note: Where Giant Skiddow , &c.]With the above- mentioned Drawings the curious reader may ∫ee three different Views of this beautiful lake, all exactly copied after nature. The fir∫t, of the whole lake, taken from Lodore, and terminated by Skiddow. The ∫econd, taken from the par∫onage-hou∫e, and terminated by Borrodale. The third, from Hill-top, with Ca∫low-cragg appearing on the foreground; and al∫o One of the ca∫cade.
poem.line: And move their hearts with ∫ofter joy.
For plea∫ures They need never roam,
Thrice happy They at home to prove
A Parent's and a Brother's love,
Her bright example pleas'd to trace,
Which lu∫tre give in female life
And ri∫ing far o'er grief and pain,
The glories of her race maintain.
THEIR ancient feats lets other fly
While, hopele∫s of their lord's return,
From Lowther She di∫tains to run
Welcomes the friend, relieves the poor,
And early know and love their lord
Who∫e courteous deeds to all extend,
And make each happy gue∫t a friend.
In ∫howers on hill and dale and plain.
O May the virtues, which adorn
With mode∫t beams his ri∫ing morn,
May he with bounty's brighte∫t ray
With arts improve, reward their toil,
Glad with kind warmth our northern ∫ky,
poem.note: __ enrich the ∫oil &c.] The late Lord Lon∫dale ∫pared no expence of money or time to introduce woollen and linen Manufactures into the county of We∫tmoreland; to improve the native in eth art of hu∫bandry by his own example, and encourage them by ∫uitable rewards. Be∫ides conferring premiums on tho∫e who excell'd, he al∫o, in order to conquer the forces of ignorance and prejudice, more ob∫tinate than perhaps the ∫oil, apprenticed out into neigbouring counties, which were more ∫killed in agriculture, ∫everal ∫ons of his tenants for that laudable purpo∫e; and laid them under obligation to return again, and exerci∫e that Art, for a certain term in their own country.

chap.p: HERE the Author thinks him∫elf bound to acknowledge, that he owes the Explanatory Notes, on the de∫cription of the mines to Dr, Brownrigg of Whitehaven. The kind and friendly de∫ign with which they were ∫ent to him, will be∫t appear from the letter which accompany'd them; and which is here ∫ubjoined. If the inqui∫itive reader ∫hould de∫ire to ∫ee a larger ∫pecimen of that Gentleman's knowledge of philo∫ophical and commercial ∫ubjects, he would recommend him to a treati∫e entitled “The art of making Common Salt, as now practi∫ed in “ mo∫t parts of the world; with ∫everal improvements propo∫ed in that art, for the “u∫e of the Briti∫h dominions, by William Brownrigg, M.D. and F.R.S.” but that it is now he believes out of print. However he may have his curio∫ity in ∫ome degree gratified by a good account of that work, given by a Mr. Wat∫on in the Philo∫ophical Tran∫actions, No 487, for the months of April, may and part of June, 1748.

chap.title: A LETTER TO THE AUTHOR
chap.head: A LETTER to the AUTHOR.
SIR,
chap.p: I give you thanks for the plea∫ure I have received in the peru∫al of your poem, heightened perhaps by a fondne∫s for every thing that you have there ∫o eloquently de∫cribed. I am however apprehen∫ive, that ∫uch of your readers as are unacquainted with your ∫ubject, may not have the ∫ame reli∫h for ∫everal parts of your performance. Much of the plea∫ure which we receive from de∫criptions of the country mu∫t ari∫e from recalling to mind tho∫e rural ∫cenes that have given us delight, and from comparing them with their repre∫entations; and ob∫erving with what art and judgement tho∫e repre∫entations are copied after nature. And altho' the ∫cenes delineated in your poetic land ∫kips, ∫eem as beautifully varied, and as well adapted to give plea∫ure to the judicious as tho∫e that are mo∫t admired in other countries, and may ∫erve as excellent models for the embelli∫hment of rural ∫ituations: yet it mu∫t be owned that, in this part of your poem, you labour under ∫ome di∫advantage, from the choice of your ∫ubject in a retired part; which does not fall ∫o much under the eye of the curious as Wind∫or Fore∫t and ∫ome other places, who∫e charms have been di∫played by ∫ome of our be∫t poets. However, very happily for you, though your Brother has devoted the large∫t ∫hare of his time and ∫tudy this ∫ummer to adorning our New Church with his Painting, yet he has found lei∫ure to make very exact Drawings of the paces your de∫cribe. The∫e, as they are the be∫t comment on this part of your work, will, I hope, in a great mea∫ure remove the difficulty here hinted at; and the Public will have the plea∫ure of ∫eeing the ∫i∫ter arts mutually reflecting light upon each other, and con∫piring, by a friendly emulation, to ∫et off the∫e beautiful ∫cenes to the be∫t advantage.

Another part of your performance will, I am afraid, be attended with greater difficulties. Your de∫criptions of the country mu∫t be generally under∫tood; and, like a fine picture, will be admired by many who do not know the original; although they will be read with mo∫t delight by tho∫e who are be∫t acquainted with your ∫ubject. But few of your readers will have ∫uch a knowledge of mines as will enable them to follow you through their dark and intricate labyrinths. More e∫pecially, as the∫e are a ∫ubject that has not, I think, before been attempted in ver∫e. And yet they ∫eem well to de∫erve the notice of our poets, as
they abound in objects proper to excite admiration, and are one great ∫ource of the wealth and power of the∫e kingdoms. Here it may be worth the while to ∫top a little, and reflect on the labour and dangers that They ∫u∫tain, who, from the mines ∫upply us with many nece∫∫aries and conveniences of life: what multitudes of people by them are maintained: what efforts of human rea∫on are there exerted, in the mo∫t ingenious inventions: and what immen∫e trea∫ures are thence rai∫ed, by which numberle∫s wheels are ∫et in motion in the complicated machine of commerce. the ∫ubterranean regions, hitherto delineated y the luxuriant fancies of poets, are widely different from the∫e great funds of trea∫ure. And as the veracity of tho∫e poets, who have de∫cended into the lower regions, hath often been called in que∫tion, ∫ome may even ∫u∫pect that you al∫o have indulged your∫elf in this poetic licence, and have related ∫uch things of the∫e darks abodes as would be∫t appear in ver∫e, rather than as you really found them in nature. To obviate which ∫u∫picions, may it not be nece∫∫ary to produce authentic vouchers of your having faithfully de∫cribed ∫uch objects as occurred to you in the coal-mines? Had Cervantes taken this method, his wonderful account of a certain cave would perhaps have met with more credit than it now does, notwith∫tanding his artful in∫inuation of its having been believed by a very great ∫cholar. The Explanatory Notes, which, agreeable to your reque∫t I ∫end enclo∫ed, and which you are at liberty to publi∫h with your poem, may ∫erve as a ∫ort of circum∫tantial proof of the truth of your de∫criptions. You will readily perceive that the nature of your de∫ign would not allow me to write a hi∫tory of collieries, or a philo∫ophical di∫∫ertation on damps. I have therefore contented my∫elf with relating a few facts which may throw ∫ome light on this part of your poem, and may help to render you de∫cription of the mines intelligible to your readers.

chap.title: SOME THOUGHTS ON BUILDING AND PLANTING TO SIR JAMES LOWTHER
chap.head: SOME THOUGHTS ON BUILDING AND PLANTING TO Sir JAMES LOWTHER of LOWTHER-HALL, Bart.
TO Sir JAMES LOWTHER, Bart.

poem.line: Worthy the Owner and the Place,
Fa∫hion will not the works direct,
The Doric grave, where weight requires,
poem.note: The Doric Grave, where weight requires.]In ea aede cum volu∫∫ent columnas collocare, non habentes ∫ymmetrias earum, & quaerentes quibus rationibus efficere po∫∫ent, ut & ad onus ferendum e∫∫et idonae, & in a∫pectu probatam haberent venu∫tatem: dimen∫i ∫unt virilis pedis ve∫tigium, & cum inveni∫∫ent pedem ∫extam partem a∫∫e altitudinis in homine, ita in columnam tran∫tulerunt: & qua cra∫∫itudine fecerunt ba∫in ∫capi, tantum eam fexies cum capitulo in altitudinem extulerunt. Ita Dorica colmna virilis corporis proportionem, & firmutatem & venu∫tatem inaedificiis prae∫tare coepit. Vitruv.L.IV C.i p.60
poem.line: THESE their abundant aid will lend
To a building can a mode belong
But Gay, or Delicate, or Strong?
poem.note: The light Corinthian, &c.] tertium vero, quod Corinthium dicitur, viginalis habet gracilitatis imitationem; quod virgines propter aetatis teneritatem gracilioribus membris figuratae, effectus recipiunt in ornatu venu∫tiores. Ejus qutum capituli prima inventio. etc. Ibid.

Between them ∫ee, &c.] Junoni, Dianae, Libero Patri, caeterifq; Diis qui eadem ∫unt ∫imilitudine, ∫i aedes Ionicae con∫truerentur, habita erit ratio mediocritatis, quid & ab fevero more Doricorum & a teneritate Corinthiorum, temperabitur earum in∫titutio proprietatis. Ibid.

Th'Ionic, &c.]Item po∫tea Dianae con∫tituere aedem quaerentes, novi generis ∫peciem, iifdem ve∫tigiis ad muliebrem tran∫tulerunt gracilitatem: & fecerunt primum columnae cra∫∫itudinem altatudinis octava parte: ut haberent ∫peciem ecel∫iorem, ba∫i ∫piram ∫uppo∫uerunt pro calceo, capitulo volutas, uti capillamento concri∫patos cincinnos praependentes dextra ac finitra collocaverunt, & cymati∫s & encarpis pro crinibus di∫po∫itis, frontes ornaverunt: truncoq; toto ∫trias, uti ∫tolarum rugas matronali more dimiferunt. Ibid.
poem.line: Why ∫earch we then for Orders new,
But that the ∫tandard rules of Greece
In every part con∫ult the whole,
Teach art to dre∫s, and not di∫gui∫e,
And, as he bids, the ∫tructure rear.
SMILES He o'er fragrant Flora's bloom?
Ne'er ∫hock him with a grotto's gloom.
poem.note: -- from real or from ∫eeming u∫e] -- quaemadmodum mutuli cantheriorum projecturae ferunt imaginem, fic in Ionicis denticuli ex projecturis a∫∫erum habent imitationem. Itaque in Graecis operibus nemo ∫ub mutulo denticulos con∫tituit: norenim po∫∫unt ∫ubtuc cantherios a∫∫eres e∫∫e. Wuod ergo ∫upra cantherios & templa in veritae debet e∫∫e collocatum, id in imaginibus, ∫i infra con∫titutum fuerit, mendo∫am habebit operis rationem: etc.
poem.line: His roughne∫s in the rugged rock.
Nor by trim ∫teps hand gently down
ALL forms ari∫e at Nature's call,
And U∫e can beauty give to all.
Non e're di∫gu∫t the judging mind,
When vary'd well, or well combin'd.
And kept it in his con∫tant view.
Nature mi∫takes them for her own,
yet all to proper foil and ∫ite
While tender plants in vales repo∫e,
Where the mild Zephyr only blows,
Who builds or plants this rule ∫hould know,
FROM TRUTH AND USE ALL BEAUTIES FLOW.

chap.note: From truth, &c.] quod non pote∫t in veritae fieri, id non putaverunt in imaginibus factum, po∫∫e certam rationem habere. Omnia emin certa proprietate, & a veris naturae deductis moribus, traduxerunt in perum perfectiones: & ea probaverunt quuorum explicationes in di∫putationibus rationem po∫∫unt habere vertitatis. Vitruv. Lib. IV. C. ii. p. 67. Edit de Laet.
and U∫e, &c.]See the Idea of Beauty explained by the great Dr. Berkley in the Minute Philo∫opher. Dial.III. Sect. vii, ix. Edit. 3. 1752.
